Before you start

Students learn that many mental health conditions start between the teens and mid-20s, that college help is opt-in, and they plan what to set up before move-in. Bring index cards, and keep the 2 a.m. friend question private. The Wes and Sam story involves suicide risk, so leave time to check in with anyone it hits.

Every student in the room

On the Lena card, say plainly that families and faiths handle mental health very differently, and that getting support doesn't mean choosing against your family's values.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Open with: “At home, somebody noticed when you skipped dinner. At college, nobody does by default. Today is about building that back on purpose.”

Slide 2 · Notes

Ask them to think, not answer. Let 20 seconds of silence sit. Then: “If your answer for next year is ‘not yet,’ that’s normal. It’s the first thing to work on.”

Slide 3 · Notes

Take a few guesses at an age. Next slide: about two in three have started by 25.

Slide 4 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 5 · Notes

These are screening surveys of symptoms, not diagnoses; say so. The point: earlier is easier.

Slide 6 · Notes

Two minutes in pairs. Small things count: waking you up, noticing you seem off, making the appointment.

Slide 7 · Notes

Take four or five. Name the pattern: most of what they listed happens without anyone asking.

Slide 8 · Notes

Most of this happened without you asking. Next slide: what changes.

Slide 9 · Notes

At 18, doctors and counselors generally can’t share health information with parents without permission. Decide with your family what you want shared; release forms exist. Ask your therapist now about crossing state lines.

Slide 10 · Notes

Pairs decide, then a couple share. Families and faiths handle mental health very differently; getting support isn’t choosing against your family. Next slide shows one good move.

Slide 11 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 12 · Notes

Read it slowly. Asking directly doesn’t put the idea in anyone’s head. Either way, Wes walks Sam to health services about the medication; stopping some medications suddenly can make people feel worse.

Slide 13 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 14 · Notes

Lead with what students bring. Then name, without pointing at anyone, that some lists cost more to build. Counseling centers are often free or low-cost; health services can help with cost.

Slide 15 · Notes

Students pick the one they’ll do first. If phones are allowed, give 60 seconds to look up the counseling center at a school they’re considering.

Slide 16 · Notes

Use it for the call home. One small study at one school, so present it as encouraging, not a promise.

Slide 17 · Notes

Two minutes in pairs. Nobody speaks for a group.

Slide 18 · Notes

Take a few. Listen for strengths as well as costs.

Slide 19 · Notes

Share the student page link. Close with: “If any of this hit close to home today, come find us before you leave.”

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students understand why the college years are prime time for mental health problems to start, what changes when nobody signs them up for help, and leave with a short list of things to set up before move-in, starting with their 2 a.m. person.

Materials

  • Index cards, one per student
  • Phones allowed for the last step (looking up a counseling center)
  • The student page link (last slide) to share afterward

Flow

  1. 3 minWho’s your 2 a.m. friend? (private)
  2. 4 minWhy the timing matters: guess, then the first-year numbers
  3. 5 minWhat home did for you: turn and talk, share out, then your favorites list
  4. 5 minTwo stories: Lena, Wes and Sam
  5. 3 minEvery student, five things to set up, a rough start, close

Short on time (10-minute version)

The 2 a.m. friend question (2), home and college favorites (3), set up five things before move-in (5). Skip the stories or hand them out for later.

Before you teach
The 2 a.m. friend question is private.

Pause on it and let the silence work. Some students have nobody in mind, at school or at home. Say "not yet" is normal and is the first thing to work on.

Some students are already in care.

Students who see a therapist or take medication are in the room. Talk about planning the handoff as ordinary, the way you'd plan for any prescription.

Wes and Sam involve suicide risk.

Read the story slowly. Model the direct question ("Did you mean you're thinking about killing yourself?") and say plainly that asking doesn't put the idea in anyone's head. Then say what Wes does next: 988, campus safety, the RA.

Screening numbers aren't diagnoses.

The 35% and 37% figures come from screening surveys of symptoms. Say so, so nobody leaves thinking a third of college students have a disorder.

No screening questions in class.

Don't ask students to rate their own mood or history out loud. Keep it to planning.

After the lesson.

If a student tells you they're struggling or worried about a friend, follow up one on one that day.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Families talk about mental health differently.

Some families expect to know everything; some never talk about mental health; some handle problems through prayer or keeping it in the family. Present each as a starting point the student gets to work with, not a barrier to be fixed.

First in the family.

First-generation students may feel they can't say it's hard because of what their family gave up. Name first-generation offices and the line "It's been harder than I expected" as normal.

Faith as support.

For some students, a campus chaplain, a place of worship or a faith group is the natural first door. Name it alongside the counseling center.

Black students and belonging.

The Walton and Cohen study found the biggest gains for Black students. Present it as evidence that a rough start is usually a phase, not as a statement about any group's ability.

Money and insurance.

Counseling centers are often free or low-cost; outside care and prescriptions may not be. Mention that health services can help with cost so no student assumes help is out of reach.

Disability and neurodivergence.

Students with ADHD, learning differences or chronic illness lose their high school supports too. Disability services must be contacted by the student; plan that like the counseling handoff.

What the research says

Pooling 192 studies and more than 700,000 people, about a third of people who ever have a mental health condition already had symptoms by 14, and close to two-thirds by 25. The peak age of onset is mid-adolescence.

Solmi et al., 2022

35% of first-year students across 19 colleges in 8 countries screened positive for a lifetime mental health condition, and 31% for one in the past year.

Auerbach et al., WHO World Mental Health International College Student Project, 2018

In 2024 to 2025, 37% of US college students had moderate to severe depression symptoms, 32% had moderate to severe anxiety, and 52% reported high loneliness. These are screening surveys, and the numbers have improved since 2022.

Healthy Minds Study, 2024 to 2025 report

In a review of college sleep research, about half of students reported daytime sleepiness and most weren't getting enough sleep, which is tied to lower grades and worse mood.

Hershner and Chervin, 2014

First-year students who read that worries about belonging are common and fade with time did better over the next three years. Black students who got the message earned higher grades, cutting the racial achievement gap roughly in half, and reported better health. It was one small study at one school.

Walton and Cohen, Science, 2011
